name: Caffeine
lethalBasis: human estimate (about 150-200 mg/kg reported)
notes: The FDA puts toxic effects (racing heart, dangerous heart rhythms, seizures) at roughly 1.2 g, and life-threatening doses typically at 10 to 14 g, though less can be dangerous for children and sensitive people. Pure caffeine powder is far more dangerous than drinks: one teaspoon equals roughly 28 cups of coffee, and it is almost impossible to measure safely at home.

name: Table salt (sodium chloride)
lethalBasis: low end of the reported human range (0.5-1 g/kg)
notes: The daily guidance of 2,300 mg is for sodium, which equals about 5.75 g of salt (a bit under one teaspoon). Salt poisoning is a real risk, especially in small children. Never use salt water to induce vomiting. No firm threshold for toxic effects is shown because published figures vary too widely.

toxicNote: No reliable human dose threshold. Early signs are strong thirst, weakness and nausea; severe cases bring confusion, muscle twitching and seizures.

name: Alcohol (ethanol)
notes: About 0.8 g of pure ethanol per kg (roughly 3 to 4 drinks) brings a blood alcohol level of about 0.10. Drinking fast can be dangerous at far lower amounts, and children are much more vulnerable. US guidance is up to 1 drink a day for women and 2 for men. Blood alcohol is estimated from your body water (Hume and Weyers equations) and a 0.84 blood water factor, so real values vary. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911.

NIAAA: Alcohol poisoning

lethalNote: No single fatal dose can be given, because tolerance varies enormously. A clinical reference says severe intoxication can develop at about 1 to 1.5 mL of pure ethanol per kg (roughly 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg), and death is usually linked to blood levels above about 80 to 90 mmol/L (roughly 0.37 to 0.41 percent), though it can be higher in regular heavy drinkers. Children can be harmed by very small amounts. Call 911.

name: Nutmeg
notes: Normal cooking amounts are fine. Poisoning has been reported at about 5 g (roughly 2 teaspoons): nausea, racing heart, confusion, hallucinations, lasting a day or longer. Fatalities are very rare and no lethal dose is established.

safeNote: No official daily limit. Normal cooking amounts are not a concern.
lethalNote: No established fatal dose. Deaths are very rare.

name: Sugar (sucrose)
lethalBasis: rat LD50; not a realistic human figure
notes: The lethal figure comes from rats. A person could not realistically eat that much, and the real harms of sugar are long-term, not a single-dose poisoning. The guidance limit is the American Heart Association figure for added sugar for most women and children over 2 (36 g for most men).

toxicNote: Not acutely toxic to people at realistic amounts. Rats given huge doses showed sluggishness and diarrhea. The harm from sugar is long-term, not from a single dose.

name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol)
notes: The Extra Strength label limit is 6 tablets (3,000 mg) in 24 hours; other products have different limits, so check your label. Accidental overdose is common because acetaminophen is hidden in many cold, flu and sleep products. Count every source. An overdose can feel fine for the first day while liver damage develops, so call Poison Control immediately if more than directed was taken.

safeNote: This app does not give a safe daily amount for nicotine from tobacco or vapes. For quit-smoking products, follow the label (see Nicotine gum).
toxicNote: In reported cases, swallowing tobacco or nicotine gum at doses up to about 6 mg per kg caused poisoning symptoms without death. A smaller body gets a bigger dose per kg, so a swallow an adult might shrug off can poison a child.
lethalNote: The widely repeated adult fatal dose of 30 to 60 mg (about 0.5 to 1 mg per kg) traces back to dubious 19th-century self-experiments. A 2014 review in Archives of Toxicology estimates an oral LD50 of about 6.5 to 13 mg per kg instead, and notes people have survived far larger amounts. That is one toxicologist's estimate and is still debated, so do not treat it as a safe margin: any swallow, especially of concentrated e-liquid or by a child, is an emergency.
name: Nicotine
servingName: nicotine absorbed from one cigarette (about 2 mg)
notes: Smoking one cigarette takes up about 2 mg of nicotine, according to the same review. Check the label for the nicotine amount in any product. Call Poison Control right away for any swallow.

There is no simple antidote; treatment is intensive supportive care and sometimes a liver transplant. No fatal dose is established; toxicity depends on the plant part, season and the person.

notes: Do not wait for symptoms. Seek help immediately and keep a piece of the mushroom for identification. Look-alikes make wild mushrooms impossible to judge unless you are an expert, and the Western destroying angel is also dangerous. safeNote: Do not swallow, and never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or toilet bowl cleaners.
toxicNote: Typical household bleach is 4 to 8 percent sodium hypochlorite. One or two mouthfuls usually cause minor mouth and throat irritation, stomach upset and vomiting. Larger amounts or stronger types, such as pool bleach, cause worse symptoms.
lethalNote: Concentrated bleach can cause permanent damage to the stomach and gut and may result in death. No fatal dose is established.
name: Bleach
notes: Mixing bleach with ammonia makes chlorine gas, which can cause choking and serious breathing problems. If swallowed, follow Poison Control's directions; MedlinePlus says to give water or milk right away unless a provider says not to. Call 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble. Poison centers advise never storing bleach in a cup or food container.

safeNote: Not for eating. Keep pods out of sight and reach of children.
toxicNote: Biting into a pod can cause coughing, choking, trouble breathing and coma. The detergent can also irritate the skin and burn the eyes. Pods cause more stomach irritation and more breathing problems and drowsiness than liquid detergent.
lethalNote: Poison Control lists severe vomiting, severe breathing trouble, esophagus burns and coma as possible effects. No fatal dose is established.

notes: Laundry packets are more concentrated than regular detergent. Store them in the closed original container, up high or locked. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away for any swallow or exposure.

safeNote: Never swallow. Keep batteries and any device with a loose battery away from children.
toxicNote: When a battery is swallowed it is impossible to know whether it will pass or get stuck. A coin-shaped battery caught in the esophagus can cause serious burns in as little as two hours, and larger button batteries can burn a hole through the esophagus or cause death.
lethalNote: This is an emergency, not a dose question. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.
name: Button batteries
notes: If anyone swallows a battery of any size, call the National Battery Ingestion Hotline at 1-800-498-8666 (24 hours) or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 immediately, and go to the emergency room. Over 3,500 people a year in the US swallow button batteries. Watch for coughing, drooling, trouble swallowing, refusing to eat or drink, and fever. Tape over discarded button batteries before throwing them away.

notes: MedlinePlus warns metformin may rarely cause a serious, life-threatening condition called lactic acidosis. Risk is higher with kidney disease, age over 65, certain heart or liver conditions, heavy alcohol use and some other medicines. safeNote: EFSA says eating more than three small raw apricot kernels (about 370 mg) in one serving can exceed the safe level for adults. For a toddler, even one small kernel can exceed it. EFSA's safe one-off level for cyanide is 20 micrograms per kg of body weight.
toxicNote: Chewing or grinding raw apricot kernels turns amygdalin into cyanide. Cyanide poisoning can cause nausea, fever, headache, insomnia, thirst, lethargy, nervousness, aches and pains, and falling blood pressure.
lethalNote: In extreme cases cyanide poisoning is fatal. EFSA reports a lethal cyanide dose of 0.5 to 3.5 mg per kg of body weight. Kernels vary a lot in how much amygdalin they hold, so there is no safe count to rely on.
name: Apricot kernels
notes: EFSA says the apricot fruit itself is not a concern, only the kernel inside the stone. EFSA's assessment was prompted by sellers promoting 10 to 60 kernels a day as a cancer remedy; EFSA says judging cancer claims was outside its remit, and its finding is that those intakes are unsafe. If someone ate kernels and feels unwell, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

sources.title: EFSA: Apricot kernels pose risk of cyanide poisoning

safeNote: FDA advice: no matter your age, don't eat large amounts of black licorice at one time. The warning does not apply to red licorice, which has little or no licorice root.
toxicNote: The FDA says if you are 40 or older, eating 2 ounces of black licorice a day for at least two weeks could land you in the hospital with an irregular heart rhythm. The cause is glycyrrhizin, which can lower potassium and also cause high blood pressure, swelling, lethargy and congestive heart failure.
lethalNote: A New England Journal of Medicine case report describes a 54-year-old man who died of cardiac arrest after eating about a bag and a half of black licorice daily for a few weeks, as reported by ABC News. No fatal dose is established.
name: Black licorice
notes: Potassium levels usually return to normal with no permanent problems once you stop. Licorice can also interact with some medicines and supplements, so ask a health professional. If you have eaten a lot and have an irregular heartbeat or muscle weakness, stop eating it and contact your health care provider.

sources.title: American Heart Association News: Black licorice is a candy that should inspire caution

safeNote: Never eat raw or undercooked red kidney beans. Boil dried beans properly before eating or adding to dishes.
toxicNote: The FDA Bad Bug Book says as few as four or five raw beans can trigger symptoms. Illness usually begins 1 to 3 hours after eating, with extreme nausea, then vomiting that may be very severe, followed by diarrhea.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established. People normally feel better within a few hours, though some cases needed hospital care.
name: Raw kidney beans
notes: Raw red kidney beans carry 20,000 to 70,000 hemagglutinating units of the toxin phytohaemagglutinin, against 200 to 400 once fully cooked. The FDA Bad Bug Book says heating to 80 degrees C can make beans about five times more toxic than raw, and slow cookers often do not get hot enough, so beans should be boiled first. White kidney beans carry about a third as much toxin as red.

safeNote: MedlinePlus says potatoes that are not green and have had any sprouts removed are safe to eat. Never eat potatoes that are spoiled or green below the skin, and always throw away sprouts.
toxicNote: The poison is solanine, which MedlinePlus calls very toxic even in small amounts. Effects are mostly stomach and gut problems, often delayed 8 to 10 hours; nervous system effects can occur with large amounts. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, headache, hallucinations, delirium, dilated pupils and vision changes.
lethalNote: MedlinePlus says these poisonings can be very dangerous, and severe cases can bring paralysis, slow breathing, slow pulse and shock. No fatal dose is established.
name: Green potato
notes: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government notes solanine is almost not broken down by cooking, baking or other heating, so remove green parts and sprouts completely. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

safeNote: Eat only the stalks. MedlinePlus says the poison is in the leaf blade, while the stalk can be eaten.
toxicNote: MedlinePlus lists oxalic acid, and possibly anthraquinone glycosides, as the poisonous ingredients. Symptoms include burning and blisters in the mouth and throat, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, kidney stones, red-colored urine, seizures and coma.
lethalNote: Deaths have been reported but are rare, according to an older MedlinePlus version. No fatal dose is established.

safeNote: Do not give honey to a baby under 12 months old, in any form, including on a pacifier or baked into food. It is the only known way to prevent infant botulism from honey.
toxicNote: Honey can carry Clostridium botulinum spores. In babies under a year the spores can grow in the gut and make toxin, causing infant botulism. A survey cited by the University of Florida found spores in 10 percent of US honey samples.
lethalNote: Infant botulism is a serious illness. This app does not give a fatal amount for honey.
name: Honey
notes: The CDC, American Academy of Pediatrics and National Honey Board recommend no honey for infants under 12 months, according to University of Florida extension. After age one the digestive system is more mature and illness from spores is much less likely. If you think a baby has symptoms, get medical care at once.

safeNote: FDA and EPA advise people who might become pregnant, are pregnant or breastfeeding, and children to avoid king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, Gulf of Mexico tilefish and bigeye tuna. These have the highest mercury levels.
toxicNote: Mercury in fish can be harmful to the brain and nervous system if a person is exposed to too much over time, according to EPA. This is a long-term exposure risk, not a single-meal dose.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for mercury from fish.
name: High-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel)
notes: FDA and EPA advise 2 to 3 servings a week from the Best Choices list, or 1 serving from the Good Choices list. An adult serving is 4 ounces, about the palm of your hand. For children a serving is about 1 ounce at age 1 to 3, 2 ounces at 4 to 7, 3 ounces at 8 to 10 and 4 ounces at 11. Canned and fresh albacore (white) tuna and yellowfin tuna are Good Choices.

servingName: 12 oz can or bottle at about 5% alcohol (1 standard drink)
name: Beer
notes: Every figure is for pure alcohol, not the whole drink. One US standard drink holds 14 g of pure alcohol, and this amount comes from the serving named here at the typical strength. Many beers, wines, and drinks are stronger and count as more than one drink, so check the label. Never use these numbers to decide whether it is safe to drive. The 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines say 2 drinks or less a day for men and 1 or less for women, and that adults can also choose not to drink. The newer 2025-2030 guidelines no longer give a number. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911.

lethalNote: No single fatal dose can be given, because tolerance varies enormously. A clinical reference says severe intoxication can develop at about 1 to 1.5 mL of pure ethanol per kg (roughly 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg), and death is usually linked to blood levels above about 80 to 90 mmol/L (roughly 0.37 to 0.41 percent), though it can be higher in regular heavy drinkers. Children can be harmed by very small amounts. Call 911.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: Poison Control says the flowers, leaves and nectar are toxic, and honey made from the nectar can contain grayanotoxins. Common effects are mouth irritation, queasiness and vomiting. 'Mad honey' can also cause confusion, sharply lowered blood pressure and pulse, and an irregular heartbeat. Most exposures are mild.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this plant. Any swallowed amount of a plant on this list is a reason to call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: Poison Control says serious toxicity is rare and has mostly followed deliberate ingestion of large amounts, but the mad honey effects can be life-threatening. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. If any was eaten, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly.

safeNote: Do not touch it, and never eat it or burn it.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says it is dangerous to swallow antifreeze even in small amounts. The toxicity develops slowly as the body breaks down the ethylene glycol into by-products that affect blood chemistry, the nervous system and the kidneys. It tastes sweet, and a bittering agent does not stop poisonings.
lethalNote: Poison Control says even a little can cause kidney damage or death. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Antifreeze
notes: Never put it in a drink bottle. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Do not eat it, although it is usually considered non-toxic.

safeNote: Do not swallow magnets or let children play with them.

lethalNote: Poison Control says swallowed magnets have caused serious injury and even death in children. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Magnets
notes: Store magnet sets locked away. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

toxicNote: Poison Control says most hair rinses and conditioners are relatively safe, causing no toxicity or mild irritation of the mouth, throat or stomach if swallowed. More significant stomach irritation can occur with some color rinses (ammonia or hydrogen peroxide) and deep conditioners that contain cationic detergents.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says toxicity is low if sunscreen is accidentally swallowed, applied to the eyes or inhaled. It can sometimes cause skin irritation, rash and allergic contact dermatitis.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Sunscreen
notes: Poison Control says toxicity is low if sunscreen is accidentally swallowed. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

toxicNote: Poison Control's page on baby lotions and eczema creams says that if a baby swallows lotion they may have a mild upset stomach, loose stools or diarrhea. Take it away, wipe out the mouth and give a small amount of water.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: This entry reflects Poison Control's guidance for baby lotions; other lotions may differ. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

toxicNote: Poison Control says nail polish is not poisonous when used as intended, but some ingredients can be harmful if swallowed or inhaled over a long time. Swallowing it can cause nausea, vomiting and stomach pain. If it gets in the eye, rinse for at least 15 minutes.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: Rinse eyes or mouth, or get fresh air, if irritated. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

toxicNote: Poison Control says lip products should not be eaten or swallowed. In one reported case a 2-year-old ate two packets of lip balm and was advised to have a snack and watch for nausea, vomiting or diarrhea. Do not induce vomiting.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

lethalNote: Poison Control says oil-based paint can be inhaled into the lungs when swallowed, causing aspiration pneumonia. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says unintentional exposures to ant baits generally pose little risk because of their low concentration. Toddlers who taste ant bait might develop nausea and vomiting, and skin or eye contact causes irritation.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Ant bait
notes: Skin or eye irritation is possible. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed. Do not use DEET on children under 2 months.
toxicNote: Poison Control describes a case in which a child drank a repellent containing DEET and had seizures.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: Do not use DEET on infants under 2 months; follow the label. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says insecticides may be toxic on skin, in the eyes, inhaled or swallowed. Pyrethroids are less toxic to humans, with irritation the most common effect; large swallows can cause seizures, coma and respiratory arrest.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Bug spray
notes: Check the label for the active ingredient and tell Poison Control.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says lawn fertilizer is irritating and can cause stomach upset if swallowed. Some products also contain weed killers and insecticides.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Fertilizer
notes: Read the label for added weed killers or insecticides. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says chlorinating products for home pools are generally safe for swimmers when used properly. Chloramine gas irritates the respiratory tract, causing coughing and trouble breathing. Never mix bleach with an acid or ammonia product.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Pool chlorine
notes: Never mix bleach with an acid. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be eaten.
toxicNote: Poison Control says Play-Doh is not toxic. A large amount swallowed may cause a mild upset stomach, and it is a choking hazard.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Play-Doh
notes: Choking hazard for young children. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

sources.title: Poison Control: Is Play-Doh edible?

safeNote: Not meant to be eaten.
toxicNote: Poison Control says crayons are not poisonous, but a child can inhale one.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Crayons
notes: Call 911 if a child is having trouble breathing. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says glow sticks are not poisonous. If swallowed, mouth irritation and an upset stomach can occur. Rinse skin and eyes if the liquid leaks.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Glow sticks
notes: Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says ice-melt products commonly contain sodium chloride, calcium chloride, potassium chloride, magnesium chloride or urea. If swallowed they can be irritating and cause stomach distress, and on skin or paws they cause irritation and dryness.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Ice melt
notes: Check which chemical is in your product. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says ice-melt products commonly contain sodium chloride, calcium chloride, potassium chloride, magnesium chloride or urea. If swallowed they can be irritating and cause stomach distress, and on skin or paws they cause irritation and dryness.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: Check which chemical is in your product. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says spackle is not meant to be swallowed, and small amounts are safe.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Spackle
notes: Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed.
toxicNote: Poison Control says caulk is generally only a mild irritant, and serious effects are not expected from fumes, eye or hand contact, or a little in the mouth. Cured caulk is a possible choking hazard and may cause mild stomach upset.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Caulk
notes: Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

sources.title: Poison Control: What you need to know about caulk

safeNote: Not meant to be swallowed. Avoid skin and eye contact.
toxicNote: Poison Control says cement is corrosive because of its high pH, and can burn skin, eyes, mouth and lungs. Swallowing it can burn the lips, mouth, throat and stomach, with drooling, trouble swallowing or vomiting, and in some cases cement can harden in the gut and cause obstruction.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone swallowed it, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Cement
notes: Cement can harden in the gut. Wash thoroughly if it gets on skin. Keep it in its original container, out of sight and reach of children.

sources.title: Poison Control: Don't get burned by cement

safeNote: NCCIH says ashwagandha should be avoided during pregnancy and not used while breastfeeding.
toxicNote: NCCIH says there have been a number of cases, rare, linking liver injury to ashwagandha supplements. It seems to have sedative effects and may add to the effects of some sedatives and anti-anxiety drugs.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Ashwagandha
notes: No dose is given here. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Ashwagandha

safeNote: NCCIH says kava supplements have been linked to a risk of severe liver damage.
toxicNote: NCCIH says various kava products have been linked to rare cases of liver injury, some serious or even fatal, including water-based kava beverages. A 2018 review noted liver toxicity is especially possible if taken longer than 8 weeks. Commonly reported side effects include stomach upset, fatigue, headaches, muscle aches and trembling.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Kava
notes: No safe dose is established. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Kava
NCCIH: Anxiety and complementary approaches

safeNote: NCCIH says ginkgo leaf extract is likely safe for most adults in moderate amounts, and has been used safely in studies lasting as long as 6 years.
toxicNote: The most common side effects are dizziness, stomach symptoms, headache and allergic skin reactions. Ginkgo may increase bleeding risk with blood thinners such as warfarin. Fresh or roasted ginkgo seeds can be poisonous; NCCIH says fresh seeds contain ginkgotoxin, which can cause seizures and death.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Ginkgo biloba
notes: Do not eat ginkgo seeds. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Ginkgo
NCCIH: Complementary approaches for travelers

safeNote: NCCIH says it is likely safe for most adults to use E. purpurea extracts, and some mixtures, for short periods.
toxicNote: Some people have allergic reactions to echinacea, which may be severe. Few side effects were reported in studies, but one study in children linked echinacea to more rashes.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Echinacea
notes: Talk to a child's doctor before giving echinacea. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Echinacea
NCCIH: Colds, flu and complementary approaches

safeNote: NCCIH says black cohosh has been used safely in studies lasting as long as a year and is generally well tolerated.
toxicNote: NCCIH says rare cases of liver damage, some very serious, have been reported with commercial black cohosh products, and it is uncertain whether black cohosh caused them. Seek care for dark urine or fatigue. It may not be safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding, and some products contain the wrong herb.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Black cohosh
notes: People with liver disorders should consult a provider first. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Black cohosh

safeNote: NCCIH says milk thistle appears well tolerated when taken orally.
toxicNote: The most common side effects are bloating, nausea and gas. It may cause allergic reactions, and some products contain silymarin amounts different from the label or are contaminated.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Milk thistle
notes: Little is known about safety in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Milk thistle

safeNote: NCCIH says it may be unsafe to consume garcinia cambogia products.
toxicNote: NCCIH says numerous reports of liver toxicity have been made, and several cases of liver damage were severe, though this appears uncommon. Other effects include headache, nausea and diarrhea.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Garcinia cambogia
notes: May interact with some liver and serotonin-affecting drugs. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Garcinia cambogia

safeNote: The FDA banned dietary supplements containing ephedrine alkaloids in 2004 because of serious safety risks.
toxicNote: NCCIH says even at relatively low doses and in short-term use, ephedra has been linked to harmful effects such as high blood pressure and heart attack.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Ephedra
notes: Banned in U.S. dietary supplements since 2004. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Ephedra

safeNote: NCCIH says bitter orange is likely safe in the amounts commonly found in foods.
toxicNote: NIH ODS says supplements with bitter orange might not be safe and can cause chest pain, anxiety, headache, muscle and bone pain, a faster heart rate and higher blood pressure. Products often also contain caffeine.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Bitter orange
notes: Concerns are greatest when combined with other stimulants. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Bitter orange
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Dietary supplements for weight loss

safeNote: NIH ODS says yohimbe might not be safe, especially at yohimbine doses of 20 mg or higher, and to use it only with a provider's guidance.
toxicNote: NCCIH says studies have documented the risks of taking yohimbe, and the amount of yohimbine in supplements varies, with some products containing very little.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Yohimbe
notes: Selling yohimbine as an unapproved OTC treatment for erectile dysfunction is illegal in the U.S. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Yohimbe
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Dietary supplements for weight loss

safeNote: NCCIH says goldenseal might be safe for most adults in the short term, and in small studies about 3 g per day was given for short periods without serious harm. Longer-term safety is uncertain.
toxicNote: Goldenseal inhibits two major drug-metabolizing enzymes (CYP2D6 and CYP3A4), so it may raise the toxicity or change the effects of many medicines. One NCCIH-funded study found metformin levels fell about 25 percent with goldenseal.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Goldenseal
notes: Check medicine interactions first. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Goldenseal
NCCIH: Herb-drug interactions

safeNote: NCCIH says saw palmetto is well tolerated and has been used safely in studies for up to 3 years.
toxicNote: Adverse effects are mild and infrequent, and may include digestive symptoms, dizziness and headache.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Saw palmetto
notes: A 2011 trial gave up to three times the standard 320 mg daily dose without added benefit. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Saw palmetto
NCCIH: Spotlight on saw palmetto

safeNote: NCCIH says valerian is generally safe for short-term use by most adults and has been used with apparent safety at 300 to 600 mg daily for up to 6 weeks.
toxicNote: The safety of long-term use is unknown, though few people have reported negative side effects.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Valerian root
notes: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends against valerian for chronic insomnia. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Valerian

safeNote: NCCIH says red yeast rice products may not be safe; some have the same side effects as cholesterol-lowering drugs and some contain a harmful contaminant.
toxicNote: Some products contain substantial monacolin K, chemically identical to lovastatin, and can cause the same side effects and drug interactions. Some are contaminated with citrinin, which may damage the kidneys. Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Red yeast rice
notes: Monacolin K content varies widely; consumers can't tell how much a product contains. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Red yeast rice

safeNote: NCCIH says ordinary oral turmeric or curcumin, not modified for absorption, is likely safe in recommended amounts for up to 2 or 3 months.
toxicNote: NCCIH's page covers turmeric and curcumin together; formulations modified to increase absorption are treated differently.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Turmeric supplement
notes: Follow the label. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Turmeric

safeNote: NCCIH says ordinary oral turmeric or curcumin, not modified for absorption, is likely safe in recommended amounts for up to 2 or 3 months.
toxicNote: NCCIH's page covers turmeric and curcumin together; formulations modified to increase absorption are treated differently.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.

notes: Follow the label. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

sources.title: NCCIH: Turmeric

safeNote: NCCIH says cranberry taken orally is generally thought to be safe.
toxicNote: In very large amounts it can cause stomach upset and diarrhea, particularly in young children. Evidence on whether it interacts with warfarin conflicts.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for this product. If someone took too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if the person has collapsed, had a seizure, has trouble breathing or can't be woken.
name: Cranberry extract
notes: May lower the risk of recurrent UTIs in women, but is not a treatment for an existing UTI. Supplement strength varies by brand, so follow the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take medicines.

safeNote: NCCIH says raw or unripe elderberries and other parts of the elder tree, such as leaves and stems, contain poisonous cyanide-producing substances; cooking eliminates this toxin.
toxicNote: These can cause nausea, vomiting and severe diarrhea.

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Herbal tea
notes: Herbal teas such as chamomile, hibiscus and peppermint are naturally caffeine-free. An exception is yerba mate, and some blends contain cacao shells or other caffeine sources, so check the label.

sources.title: Republic of Tea: Tea and caffeine

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Rooibos tea
notes: Rooibos tastes like tea but has no caffeine.

sources.title: Tasting Table: Caffeine content of 9 types of tea

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Hibiscus tea
notes: Hibiscus tea is an herbal tea and is naturally caffeine-free.

sources.title: Republic of Tea: Tea and caffeine

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Ginger tea
notes: Plain ginger tea is an herbal tea and has no caffeine unless it is blended with tea leaves or yerba mate. Check the label.

sources.title: Republic of Tea: Tea and caffeine

safeNote: This app does not show a caffeine number for this drink because guarana content is not always on the label. The FDA cites about 400 mg of caffeine a day as an amount not generally linked to negative effects in healthy adults.
name: Guarana drink
notes: Guarana seeds are a concentrated caffeine source, and guarana in energy drinks adds to the drink's total caffeine. NCCIH notes energy drinks hold about 70 to 240 mg of caffeine per 16 oz. LiverTox says guarana has few side effects at conventional doses and is not linked to liver injury. If you follow caffeine guidelines, serious risks are not likely.

sources.title: NCCIH: Energy drinks
LiverTox: Guarana
FDA: Spilling the beans, how much caffeine is too much

safeNote: The FDA caps quinine in tonic water at 83 mg per liter. Quinine can still cause reactions in sensitive people. Ask a doctor if you take blood thinners or have had a quinine reaction.
name: Tonic water
notes: The FDA caps quinine in carbonated beverages at 83 parts per million (about 83 mg per liter, or about 29 mg in a 12 oz can). That is far below a medicine dose. Quinine can cause nausea, cramps, ringing in the ears and, rarely, serious bleeding or heart rhythm problems, mostly at medicine doses.

sources.title: eCFR: 21 CFR 172.575, quinine in beverages
Healthline: Quinine in tonic water

safeNote: No limit applies for normal drinking. Drink to thirst, and do not force large amounts of water in a short time.
toxicNote: More than a few liters in an hour or two can cause water intoxication. Call 911 for confusion, seizure or collapse.
name: Water
notes: Water is safe in normal amounts, but drinking far more than the kidneys can clear can dilute blood sodium (hyponatremia). Deaths have been reported after more than 5 liters (often 10 to 20 liters) in a few hours, and about 3 to 4 liters in under an hour can cause symptoms in healthy resting adults. Headache, nausea, confusion or seizure after heavy drinking is an emergency.

sources.title: PubMed: Death by water intoxication
PMC: The physiology, psychology and pathology of overhydration

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink. Avoid products with aloe latex and ask a doctor first if you take heart or diuretic medicines.
name: Aloe vera juice
notes: NCCIH says oral aloe latex can cause abdominal pain, cramps and diarrhea, and leaf extracts taken for weeks to years have been linked to acute hepatitis. Whole-leaf extract that was not decolorized is a possible human carcinogen (IARC). Look for decolorized, anthraquinone-free products. Prolonged laxative use can cause low potassium.

sources.title: NCCIH: Aloe vera
PMC: Aloe vera, a review of toxicity and adverse clinical effects

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink. Sports drinks suit exercise, not everyday sipping, because of sugar and sodium.
name: Gatorade
notes: One study measured Gatorade at 0.46 g of sodium and 0.125 g of potassium per liter (about 6% carbohydrate). Sports drinks have about 22 to 25 mmol of sodium per liter. Formulas change, so check the label. People with kidney disease or on a sodium or potassium limit should ask a provider.

sources.title: PMC: Age-related differences in water and sodium handling after hydration beverages
PMC: Sensory perception of an oral rehydration solution

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Powerade
notes: Sports drinks like Powerade are carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks with about 22 to 25 mmol of sodium per liter. Formulas change, so check the label. People with kidney disease or on a sodium or potassium limit should ask a provider.

sources.title: PMC: Sensory perception of an oral rehydration solution

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Sports drink
notes: Traditional sports drinks have about 22 to 25 mmol of sodium per liter, which may not match the sodium lost by endurance athletes. Check the label for sodium and sugar. People with kidney disease or on a sodium or potassium limit should ask a provider.

sources.title: PMC: Sensory perception of an oral rehydration solution
PMC: Compositional aspects of hydration beverages

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink. Follow the label or a doctor's advice, especially for infants.
name: Pedialyte
notes: A CDC report lists Pedialyte at 45 mEq of sodium per liter, and a study measured 1.035 g of sodium and 0.78 g of potassium per liter. It is made for oral rehydration, especially in children with diarrhea. Follow the label or your child's doctor for amounts.

sources.title: CDC MMWR: Management of acute diarrhea in children
PMC: Age-related differences in water and sodium handling after hydration beverages

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Electrolyte drink
notes: Hydration drinks with at least about 40 to 45 mmol of sodium per liter hold fluid better after sweating than lower-sodium sports drinks. Check the label, and ask a provider if you have kidney disease or take blood pressure medicines.

sources.title: PMC: Post-exercise rehydration in athletes
PMC: The Beverage Hydration Index

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink. Large amounts can cause cramps and loose stools.
name: Prune juice
notes: Prune juice has a mild laxative effect, linked to its sorbitol content (about 6 g per 100 g), and a trial found it helped chronic constipation without causing loose stools.

sources.title: PubMed: Chemical composition and health effects of prunes
PMC: Prune juice in chronic constipation trial

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Carrot juice
notes: Very large amounts of carrots or carrot juice can turn skin yellow-orange (carotenemia), which is harmless. A review says vitamin A poisoning does not occur from beta-carotene because the conversion is slow. Do not confuse it with jaundice.

sources.title: PubMed: Carotenemia, a review
PubMed: Carrot man, a case of excessive beta-carotene ingestion

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink. Do not rely on beet juice for blood pressure without asking your doctor.
name: Beet juice
notes: A systematic review says beetroot juice can easily push nitrate intake above the acceptable daily intake. Beets can also turn urine or stools red.

sources.title: PubMed: Benefits and risks of beetroot juice

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink.
name: Kombucha
notes: Kombucha is fermented tea. Federal law treats kombucha as an alcohol beverage if it reaches 0.5% alcohol by volume at any point, including by continued fermentation after bottling, so alcohol content can vary. Check the label, especially if you avoid alcohol or are pregnant.

sources.title: TTB: Kombucha
TTB: General requirements

safeNote: This app does not show a milligram limit for this drink. Not alcohol-free by law, only under 0.5% alcohol by volume.
name: Non-alcoholic beer
notes: Under federal rules, a beverage is non-alcoholic when it has less than 0.5% alcohol by volume, so these drinks can contain a small amount of alcohol. Check the label if you must avoid alcohol completely.

sources.title: TTB: Kombucha information and resources, FAQ

servingName: 3.5 oz glass at about 17% alcohol (1 standard drink)
name: Vermouth
notes: Every figure is for pure alcohol, not the whole drink. One US standard drink holds 14 g of pure alcohol, and this amount comes from the serving named here at the typical strength. Many beers, wines, and drinks are stronger and count as more than one drink, so check the label. Never use these numbers to decide whether it is safe to drive. The 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines say 2 drinks or less a day for men and 1 or less for women, and that adults can also choose not to drink. The newer 2025-2030 guidelines no longer give a number. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911. NIAAA gives 3 to 4 oz of fortified wine at about 17% alcohol as one standard drink.

lethalNote: No single fatal dose can be given, because tolerance varies enormously. A clinical reference says severe intoxication can develop at about 1 to 1.5 mL of pure ethanol per kg (roughly 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg), and death is usually linked to blood levels above about 80 to 90 mmol/L (roughly 0.37 to 0.41 percent), though it can be higher in regular heavy drinkers. Children can be harmed by very small amounts. Call 911.

notes: Every figure is for pure alcohol, not the whole drink. One US standard drink holds 14 g of pure alcohol, and this amount comes from the serving named here at the typical strength. Many beers, wines, and drinks are stronger and count as more than one drink, so check the label. Never use these numbers to decide whether it is safe to drive. The 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines say 2 drinks or less a day for men and 1 or less for women, and that adults can also choose not to drink. The newer 2025-2030 guidelines no longer give a number. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911. NIAAA says a mixed drink or cocktail counts as one or more standard drinks, and bar and home pours vary. A Long Island iced tea or a strong pour can hold several.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: Small ingestions can cause vomiting and diarrhea within an hour. All parts can cause poisoning.
lethalNote: Poison Control says most reports of severe symptoms from large ingestions come from animals, and 5 to 6 fruits can kill a small dog. In one human case, an 18-month-old who ate half a fruit had no symptoms.
name: Chinaberry
notes: Observe for GI upset for 8 hours after small ingestions per Poison Control. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: Contains tremetol, a mixture linked to trembles in livestock and milk sickness in people who drank milk from cows that ate it. Drying does not always remove toxicity: goats were poisoned by plant stored for 5 years.
lethalNote: No human dose is established. The toxin has not been proven in live animals and the toxic agent may be a metabolite.
name: White snakeroot
notes: Historically a cause of many human poisonings in the 1800s American Midwest. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: All parts, especially tubers and seeds, contain colchicine. Poisoning causes severe vomiting and diarrhea, shock, multi-organ failure and delayed bone marrow effects.
lethalNote: A fatal colchicine case report reported death after 61 hours with severe diarrhea, shock, ARDS and multiorgan failure.
name: Climbing lily
notes: Tubers resemble sweet potato or yam. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: Seeds contain strychnine and brucine. Symptoms begin within hours: anxiety, agitation, twitching and muscle spasms progressing to convulsions while conscious.
lethalNote: Strychnine causes muscle spasms and rigidity that can lead to respiratory failure and death.
name: Strychnine tree
notes: Nux vomica is banned or restricted in most countries. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: Do not touch the sap, and wear eye protection when pruning.
toxicNote: The milky sap is very irritating to skin, eyes and mouth. Eye exposure can begin to hurt immediately and can cause serious injury.
lethalNote: StatPearls says eye damage can progress to blindness without prompt treatment.
name: Euphorbia
notes: Flush skin and eyes with water immediately and keep rinsing. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: ASPCA lists kalanchoe as toxic to dogs and cats, with vomiting, diarrhea and, rarely, abnormal heart rhythm. The toxins are bufadienolides, a type of cardiac glycoside.
lethalNote: No human dose is established. Related Crassulaceae cause chronic neurotoxic poisoning in grazing livestock.
name: Kalanchoe
notes: Mainly a pet and livestock hazard. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: Do not eat. Keep away from pets and young children.
toxicNote: Contains saponins. ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs and cats, causing nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established; serious poisoning is not expected.
name: Snake plant
notes: Mild stomach upset is the typical effect. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: Do not eat, especially the tubers. Keep from pets and children.
toxicNote: Terpenoid saponins cause salivation, vomiting and diarrhea. ASPCA says large ingestions of tubers in pets can cause heart rhythm abnormalities, seizures and death.
lethalNote: Pet data: large tuber ingestions can be fatal. Human data are limited.
name: Cyclamen
notes: Tubers contain the highest concentration of toxin. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: Eating the whole leaf or the yellow latex under the skin is not advised.
toxicNote: The leaf latex contains anthraquinones. Ingestion is associated with diarrhea, low potassium, abdominal pain and, with prolonged use, kidney failure and a dilated, poorly working colon.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established. Aloe vera whole leaf extract showed clear evidence of carcinogenic activity in rats, according to a toxicity review.
name: Aloe (plant)
notes: Gel from the inner leaf is different from the latex. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it. The flowering ornamental is not a food pea.
toxicNote: The seeds contain a lathyrogen, gamma-glutamyl-beta-aminopropionitrile, that interferes with collagen and causes skeletal deformities and aortic rupture in animals.
lethalNote: Human poisoning from ornamental sweet peas is not well documented.
name: Sweet pea
notes: Eating large amounts over a long time is the concern. Avoid eating the seeds or pods. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: Do not eat the leaves or stems. Ripe tomato fruit is fine.
toxicNote: Leaves, stems and unripe fruit contain alpha-tomatine, a steroidal glycoalkaloid. Glycoalkaloid doses of 1 to 5 mg/kg are acutely toxic to humans.
lethalNote: Doses of 3 to 6 mg/kg of glycoalkaloids have resulted in death, according to a food-toxin review (potato data).
name: Tomato leaves
notes: Cooking does not destroy glycoalkaloids. Tomatine is much less toxic than solanine in practice. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: Do not eat the leaves, sprouts or green tubers.
toxicNote: Potato tops contain much higher glycoalkaloids than tubers. In a UK study, leaf samples had up to 22.6 mg alpha-solanine and up to 55.7 mg alpha-chaconine per 100 g.
lethalNote: Glycoalkaloid doses of 1 to 5 mg/kg are acutely toxic and 3 to 6 mg/kg have resulted in death, per a food-toxin review.
name: Potato leaves
notes: Tubers kept from light contained only 0.05 to 0.65 mg alpha-solanine per 100 g. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: Avoid completely with kidney disease. Otherwise limit to small servings and do not eat on an empty stomach.
toxicNote: Contains caramboxin, a neurotoxin, and oxalate. In people with impaired kidneys it can cause hiccups, confusion, seizures and status epilepticus. Oxalate can also cause acute kidney injury.
lethalNote: Starfruit toxicity can cause severe and often fatal encephalopathy in kidney failure patients, even after small amounts. One man who ate more than 50 starfruit needed dialysis.
name: Starfruit (kidney risk)
notes: People with normal kidneys usually clear the toxin, but dehydration and an empty stomach raise the risk. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 and name the plant exactly. Call 911 for seizures, collapse or trouble breathing.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it. Do not apply bloodroot or black salve to skin.
toxicNote: The root contains sanguinarine, which kills cells by blocking Na+/K+-ATPase. On skin it forms an eschar (dead tissue), and bloodroot products can cause significant tissue destruction and keloid scarring. StatPearls says swallowed sanguinarine may induce heart failure and myocarditis.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established.
name: Bloodroot
notes: Black salve is advertised as a skin cancer cure but clinical evidence is lacking and it destroys healthy tissue too. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: Contains insoluble calcium oxalate crystals. Chewing causes oral irritation, pain and swelling of mouth, tongue and lips, drooling, vomiting and difficulty swallowing (ASPCA lists it as toxic to dogs, cats and horses).
lethalNote: Serious poisoning is not expected.
name: Skunk cabbage
notes: Rinse the mouth and sip water or milk; call Poison Control if swelling affects swallowing or breathing. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it. Keep from pets and children.
toxicNote: ASPCA lists the ZZ plant among insoluble calcium oxalate houseplants. Chewing causes mouth and throat irritation, drooling, vomiting and diarrhea.
lethalNote: Serious poisoning is not expected.

safeNote: Do not eat garden mums.
toxicNote: ASPCA lists chrysanthemum as toxic to dogs, cats and horses. Toxins are sesquiterpene lactones and pyrethrins, causing vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, incoordination and skin irritation.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established.
name: Chrysanthemum
notes: Mostly a pet hazard; contact dermatitis can occur in people. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: There is no safe amount to eat. Do not eat it.
toxicNote: A case-report review groups Boston ivy among plants with soluble oxalates, which can cause systemic oxalate toxicity (kidney effects) when eaten in quantity.

notes: Berries attract children; swallowing small amounts is usually mild. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: Do not swallow. Keep out of children's reach.
toxicNote: MedlinePlus lists aluminum salts and ethyl alcohol as the harmful ingredients. Swallowing can cause throat burning, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, blurred vision, slurred speech, low blood pressure and, with large amounts, collapse. Eye contact can burn.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established.
name: Deodorant
notes: Do not make the person throw up unless told to. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: Do not swallow. Keep out of children's reach.
toxicNote: MedlinePlus says shaving cream is not very poisonous; most symptoms come from allergic reaction or eye contact. Ingredients of concern are anionic and nonionic surfactants. Symptoms can include throat burning, stomach pain, vomiting, rash and blurred vision.
lethalNote: Recovery is very likely.
name: Shaving cream
notes: Rinse eyes with water for 15 minutes if splashed. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: Do not eat. Keep candles away from toddlers.
toxicNote: MedlinePlus considers candle wax nonpoisonous, but a large amount swallowed may block the intestines. Scents and dyes can cause allergic reactions.
lethalNote: Recovery is very likely.
name: Candles
notes: Burning candles pose fire and indoor-air hazards separate from swallowing. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: Do not swallow tablets or the soaking solution. Rinse dentures well.
toxicNote: In a case report, a man who swallowed three denture cleanser tablets developed a perforated gastric ulcer within 7 days; authors say intact tablet fragments likely cause significant stomach injury, while dissolved tablets are less likely to. Consumer reports describe burning mouth and upset stomach after swallowing solution.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established.
name: Denture cleaner
notes: Ingesting whole tablets is more hazardous than the dissolved liquid. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: Use only as directed for lenses. Never put hydrogen peroxide solution directly in the eye.
toxicNote: Poison Control says swallowing contact lens solution can cause nausea, mild stomach upset and burning in the mouth and throat. Hydrogen peroxide solution in the eye causes chemical burns.
lethalNote: Serious poisoning from swallowing is not expected.
name: Contact lens solution
notes: Peroxide and rinse solutions come in similar bottles; check the label every time. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.

safeNote: Swish and spit. Do not give to children who may swallow.
toxicNote: Poison Control says swallowing a mouthful is unlikely to cause toxicity, but large amounts can cause toxicity from alcohol and/or fluoride: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, blood electrolyte changes and kidney and heart problems. ATSDR says rinses contain high fluoride and are not intended to be ingested.
lethalNote: One review gives a probably toxic fluoride dose of about 5 mg/kg for children and an acute lethal dose of 32 to 64 mg/kg for adults.
name: Fluoride rinse
notes: Call Poison Control for any child who swallows more than a mouthful. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble, and 911 if the person has collapsed, is seizing or can't be woken.
